summaryEn: Hoya visits Heungdeoksa Temple in Cheongju, where Jikji was printed with metal movable type in 1377. It is the world's oldest surviving book of its kind, and its one remaining volume is kept in Paris.
learningGoalsEn: Understand what movable metal type is: one small piece of type for each character, lined up to print a page.
Know that Jikji was printed in 1377 at Heungdeoksa Temple in Cheongju and is the world's oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
Know where the surviving volume is kept today (the National Library of France) and that it was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2001.
Read and recognize 절 (jeol), 스님 (seunim), 제자 (jeja), 활자 (hwalja), 금속활자 (geumsokhwalja) and 박물관 (bangmulgwan).

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

the second (last) volume of a set

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya travels to Cheongju in the time of the Goryeo kingdom. At Heungdeoksa Temple, people are busy with something amazing: printing a book with metal type!
scenes.artBrief: A peaceful Goryeo-era temple courtyard with a wooden hall and a stone pagoda; inside an open door, figures bend over a work table with small shiny pieces. Hoya peeks around a pillar.
scenes.captionEn: Printing with metal type at a temple

scenes.narrationEn: The book is called Jikji. In 1372, a wise old monk named Baegun, then 75 years old, gathered important teachings of the Buddha and great teachers into it.
scenes.artBrief: An elderly monk in gray robes writing calmly with a brush at a low desk by a paper window; mountains outside. No readable text on the paper.

scenes.narrationEn: In 1377, Baegun's students printed the book here, with support from a Buddhist nun named Myodeok.
scenes.artBrief: Two younger monks carefully lifting a freshly printed sheet (shown as soft gray lines, no readable text) while a nun in robes watches kindly.

scenes.narrationEn: How does it work? Each character is its own little piece of metal type. Printers line the pieces up to make a page, then print it. Metal type made printing easier, and mistakes easier to fix.

keyword.en: printing type (one piece for each character)

scenes.artBrief: Close-up of hands placing tiny metal blocks into a tray frame in neat rows (block faces shown blank or as abstract bumps); Hoya holds one tiny block up to the light.
scenes.captionEn: One piece of type for each character

scenes.narrationEn: Jikji is the oldest surviving book in the world printed with movable metal type. Old records show metal type was used in Goryeo even earlier, but Jikji is the oldest such book that still exists.
scenes.artBrief: Hoya proudly holds up an old bound book like a trophy on a small hill, with a gentle golden glow behind him; the cover is plain.

scenes.narrationEn: The book had two volumes. Only the second volume survives today, and it is kept at the National Library of France in Paris.

keyword.en: the second (last) volume of a set

scenes.artBrief: A quiet, grand library reading room with tall shelves and arched windows; one old book rests safely in a protective case. No signs, no flags, no text.

scenes.narrationEn: In 2001, UNESCO added Jikji to the Memory of the World Register. UNESCO also has a prize carrying its name, for people who help protect old documents and share them.
scenes.artBrief: Hoya and children around the world holding hands in a circle around a glowing old book floating above a globe. No text.

scenes.narrationEn: Heungdeoksa seems to have closed after a fire long ago. But in 1985, archaeologists digging at the site found a metal piece carved with the name Heungdeoksa, so its site was confirmed. Today the Cheongju Early Printing Museum stands beside it.
scenes.artBrief: Present day: a grassy temple site with stone foundations and a rebuilt hall, and a modern museum building nearby; Hoya waves to visiting families. No signs or text.
scenes.captionEn: A museum stands by the temple site

facts.claimEn: Baegun's disciples, including Seokchan, printed it with donations from the Buddhist nun Myodeok. The second disciple's name is written Daldam (달담) on 국가유산포털 and Daljam (달잠) on the Cheongju Early Printing Museum page, so the story does not name him.

sources.title: 유네스코 등재유산 소개 — 세계기록유산 「직지심체요절」

facts.claimEn: In movable-type printing, separate pieces of type are arranged (typeset) into a plate to print pages. Metal type made printing more convenient and economical, and it made corrections easier.
facts.claimKo: 활자 인쇄는 낱낱의 활자를 원고에 따라 배열(조판)해 판을 만들어 찍는 방식이며, 금속활자는 인쇄를 더 편리하고 경제적으로 만들고 교정을 쉽게 해 주었다.

facts.claimEn: Heungdeoksa appears to have been abandoned after a fire in late Goryeo. Its site was confirmed in 1985, when an archaeological excavation found a metal piece (geumgu) inscribed 'Heungdeoksa'. The Cheongju Early Printing Museum stands beside the site today.

verification.notes: Third independent pass. Every cited URL for all 6 episodes (52 facts) was re-opened (UNESCO pages via Wayback copies when the live site resets connections) and quotes/locators were compared; the one exception is unesco.org/en/prizes/literacy (unreachable from here; its claim is now also backed by a Korean MCST press release). Eight minimal corrections were made: (1) Hangeul Day f3 no longer says 'Gregorian' (no cited source says the October 9 conversion was Gregorian; encykorea separates Julian/Gregorian only for 1932-45) and dates the October 29/28 observances; (2) f10 gains a third source (SBS 2018 with 국립한글박물관 curator); (3) Shapes scene 8, learning goal and f7 now say 'South Korea's spelling rules' count 24 (North Korea counts 40, 국립한글박물관 webzine 59); (4) Sejong scene 4/f4: 백성 is 'an old-fashioned word' with 표준국어대사전 added; (5) Jikji f8 quote no longer repeats a prize amount that differs between UNESCO page versions; (6) Tripitaka f6 wood and corner plates now have two further sources (정책브리핑; 박상진 wood-identification study); (8) Hangeul Day f9 gains a second source (문화체육관광부 press release); (7) Panjeon scene 8/f9: 'visitors cannot walk inside' replaced by 'visitor entry is restricted' because Haeinsa has run pre-booked tours inside Beopbojeon since June 2021. See hangul-printing.signoff.md.

authorNotes: There is no comparison with Gutenberg because official Korean sources give different gaps: '70여년' and '80여년' on the 국가유산포털 Jikji page, and '78년' on the Heungdeoksa site signboard text. How the book reached France is left out as a sensitive topic for young learners; per 국가유산포털 it was collected by Collin de Plancy, passed to Henri Vever, and went to the BnF under his will after his death in 1950. It can be added later with that source. The 1972 'International Book Year' exhibition and the old misnomer 'Jikji Simgyeong' are also left out. The surviving volume has lost its first leaf (38 of 39 leaves remain, per 국가유산포털), which is left out too. The casting method (wax versus sand) is not described because it is debated, and earlier metal-type evidence (the 1239 colophon) is mentioned only in general terms. The full title is 백운화상초록불조직지심체요절 (Baegun Hwasang Chorok Buljo Jikji Simche Yojeol). REVISED: the names of Baegun's disciples are no longer given in the narration. 국가유산포털 writes the second disciple 달담 and the Cheongju Early Printing Museum writes 달잠 (達湛); the museum names Seokchan and Daljam as disciples and Myodeok as donor. Scene 8: 'diggers' -> 'archaeologists'; 'The temple itself disappeared long ago' -> 'seems to have been lost in a fire long ago' (encykorea: 폐사된 것으로 보이며); 'bronze piece' -> 'metal piece' because 국가유산포털 describes the 금구 as a 쇠북(금구) fragment. Vocab 종이/인쇄/금속 replaced by 제자/금속활자/직지 so that every vocab word appears in a scene. FINAL PASS (3rd check): f8 quote no longer repeats the prize amount (UNESCO page copies show US$ 30,000 and US$ 40,000 at different times). All other facts re-verified unchanged. REVIEW PASS (PR 1.8b): title.en and s1 say 'metal type', not 'letters made of metal' (Jikji predates Hangul and its type pieces are characters). s8 now says the temple seems to have closed after a fire (f9: abandoned after a fire). Advisory: the fire in s8 (proposed in F-STORY-001 §3.6) was reviewed and cleared; the scene names no person, harm or danger, only that a building closed long ago.
